item.title: MultiAlloc: Budget-Aware Precision Allocation for KV Cache Quantization
item.guid: title:multialloc budget aware precision allocation for kv cache quantization
item.description: The Key-Value (KV) cache constitutes a dominant source of memory consumption during large language model (LLM) inference, particularly in long-context and complex reasoning scenarios. Existing KV cache quantization methods have explored different compression granularities, including layer-wise precision adjustment and token-level information preservation. In practical deployment, however, the key challenge is not merely compression, but how to allocate limited quantization resources among heterogeneous precision preservation strategies under a fixed KV cache memory budget. We propose MultiAlloc, a profiling-guided precision allocation framework for KV cache quantization that adaptively distributes limited quantization resources between layer-wise precision enhancement and token-wise preservation. MultiAlloc employs lightweight offline profiling to characterize layer sensitivity and token importance, enabling adaptive precision allocation under a fixed memory constraint. Guided by the profiled memory--accuracy trade-off, it automatically derives an effective precision allocation strategy without online allocation search, and applies the resulting policy during inference.

item.title: MERIT: Multimodal Evidence Reasoning over Image Tables
item.guid: title:merit multimodal evidence reasoning over image tables
item.description: Table reasoning with language models typically assumes access to clean textual tables. In practice, tables are often serialized into text, which can corrupt cell contents, distort structural relationships, and discard visual cues, leaving the model to reason over incomplete evidence. In contrast, table images retain this information, but using it requires both accurate perception and reasoning grounded in the relevant cells. To address this, we propose MERIT (Multimodal Evidence Reasoning over Image Tables), a three-stage framework for learning to reason over table images, with serialized tables serving as optional auxiliary inputs (if provided). Our analysis identifies visual evidence acquisition as a bottleneck, motivating table-specific encoder adaptation through reconstruction, localization, and color-conditioned supervision. Building on the adapted representations, supervised fine-tuning teaches explicit evidence selection and reasoning using verified trajectories.

item.title: ECMR: Evidence-Aware Deliberation Control for Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning
item.guid: title:ecmr evidence aware deliberation control for multi agent llm reasoning
item.description: Multi-agent Large Language Model (LLM) systems typically commit to a deliberation protocol before inference. A fixed protocol cannot allocate computation differently to resolved and unresolved instances, and it may mistake repeated support for independent confirmation. We study this failure as semantic false consensus: a confident group answer supported by narrow, duplicated, or correlated rationales. We introduce ECMR, an evidence-aware controller over frozen role-conditioned LLMs. At each step, ECMR summarizes answer concentration, support diversity and independence, contradictions, role behavior, verification history, and remaining budget, then selects whether to propose, challenge, verify, arbitrate, diversify, correct a role, or stop. We formulate this decision as finite-horizon budgeted control and derive sufficient conditions under which state conditioning, risk-triggered verification, and role correction improve cost-adjusted utility.

item.title: PaceReasoner: Label-Free Learning to Answer Briefly from Long Reasoning
item.guid: title:pacereasoner label free learning to answer briefly from long reasoning
item.description: Extended chain-of-thought reasoning improves problem-solving performance but increases inference cost and latency, motivating more accurate answers with shorter reasoning. We introduce PaceReasoner, a label-free test-time reinforcement learning framework that uses a model's LONG responses to improve its SHORT-mode accuracy. Both modes share a trainable policy, creating a need for reliable supervision, sufficient SHORT training samples, and continued LONG responses to guide learning. PaceReasoner combines all-response and LONG-only answer consensus through progressive, confidence-weighted supervision. A behavior reward gradually shifts from encouraging SHORT exploration to rewarding agreement with LONG answers, while a ratio controller regulates the balance between modes. Across three model backbones and four benchmarks, PaceReasoner improves average SHORT accuracy over the baselines by 7.

item.title: PixelMoE: Scaling Pixel-Space Diffusion with LLM-Style Mixture-of-Experts
item.guid: title:pixelmoe scaling pixel space diffusion with llm style mixture of experts
item.description: Pixel-space diffusion models provide an appealing alternative to latent-space diffusion models by directly modeling raw images without relying on a learned tokenizer. However, scaling pixel-space models has predominantly followed dense strategies, tightly coupling model capacity with active computation. In this work, we show that standard LLM-style Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures can be effectively transferred to pixel-space diffusion. Building on this finding, we introduce PixelMoE, a pixel-space generative framework that sparsely scales model capacity with standard LLM-style MoE, without diffusion-specific routing mechanisms or auxiliary routing objectives. Specifically, PixelMoE combines standard Token-Choice (TC) routing with fine-grained routed experts for input-adaptive sparse computation, a shared expert for capturing common representations, and a bias-based load-balancing strategy. To complement sparse capacity scaling, PixelMoE further introduces Pixel-Space Hierarchical Flow Matching, which varies spatial resolution along the denoising trajectory from global structure formation to fine-grained detail refinement.

item.title: Two Routes to Interoceptive Prioritisation: Dissociating Likelihood Precision and Preference Reweighting in Active Inference
item.guid: title:two routes to interoceptive prioritisation dissociating likelihood precision and preference reweighting in active inference
item.description: An embodied agent must prioritise among competing bodily needs. In active inference, it can respond to an urgent need by increasing the precision of information about that need or by increasing its preference for outcomes that relieve it. We compare these two interventions, separately and together, in a foraging gridworld with three lethal needs, and ask how each changes survival, perception and the body model the agent learns. Precision sharpens interoceptive posteriors and improves survival. Preference reweighting keeps bodily states further from their lethal boundaries and changes the states from which the agent learns, so its learned model covers fewer need levels, with lower quality across all levels but slightly higher quality on the levels it visits. An experiment on 72 further layouts does not establish the predicted preference benefit on difficult layouts, but both interventions improve average survival there and their interaction is positive.

item.title: Beyond Answer Voting: Fine-Grained Correction of LLM Reasoning through Graph Alignment across Sampled Traces
item.guid: title:beyond answer voting fine grained correction of llm reasoning through graph alignment across sampled traces
item.description: Large language models increasingly tackle tasks that require multi-step reasoning, where errors in intermediate claims can affect the final answer. Self-consistency (SC) improves reasoning by voting over sampled final answers, but its vote leaves intermediate disagreements unresolved. To address this problem, we introduce DDRG (Disagreement-Driven Verification Guided by Reasoning Graphs), a framework for selective correction from a frozen bank of reasoning traces. Our insight is that graph alignment can expose claim-level disagreements and provide correction evidence without expanding the sampled trace bank. DDRG builds source-grounded claim graphs and sends localized conflicts to an answer-blind verifier. A verifier-supported refutation that reaches the majority answer's supporting path triggers one focused repair; otherwise, DDRG returns the exact SC vote.

item.title: ACCRUE: Continual Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Robot Foundation Models
item.guid: title:accrue continual off policy reinforcement learning for robot foundation models
item.description: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves robot foundation models (RFMs) beyond their demonstrations, but real-world deployment demands more: learning new tasks efficiently while retaining previously acquired behaviors. Existing continual RL methods on top of VLAs mitigate forgetting but rely on on-policy updates with limited forward transfer, whereas off-policy methods improve single-task sample efficiency without addressing learner persistence across tasks. We propose ACCRUE, a continual off-policy RL framework that carries lightweight actor and critic networks across tasks, allowing each stage to reuse behavioral and value knowledge acquired through prior RL. The inherited critic adapts only on current-task transitions and guides current-task actor learning, while prior behavior is preserved by distilling the actor toward cached targets on a small number of retained episodes. Fixed visual features keep the inherited learner and its replay compatible with base-policy updates. Across contact-rich assembly sequences in simulation and on real-robot hardware, ACCRUE accelerates subsequent-task learning with near-zero forgetting and significantly reduces real-robot training time by 31.

item.title: ProTok: Unified Protein Tokenization via Modular Multi-Codebook Quantization
item.guid: title:protok unified protein tokenization via modular multi codebook quantization
item.description: Protein sequence, structure, and functional annotations each capture complementary aspects of protein biology, yet existing tokenizers encode each modality independently, limiting the expressiveness of discrete protein representations. We present ProTok, a unified protein tokenizer that maps all three modalities into a modular discrete vocabulary via product quantization with per-modality codebook groups and modality dropout. A single ProTok checkpoint supports flexible inference from any modality subset without retraining. On seven StructTokenBench benchmarks spanning 14 tasks and 28 test splits, ProTok achieves an average rank of 1. 4 across all structure-only tokenizers, placing first on 21 splits and among the top two on 27 of the 28. These gains come without sacrificing reconstruction: ProTok's tokens reach 0.

item.title: Do Factuality Methods Make LLMs More Factual? Reproducibility and Fair Comparison
item.guid: title:do factuality methods make llms more factual reproducibility and fair comparison
item.description: Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to human preferences, after pre-training and supervised fine-tuning steps. However, standard RL alignment steps such as RLHF do not focus on factuality of LLMs, hence they may generate non-factual information, which could result in unintended consequences. In response, a number of factuality alignment approaches have been proposed in the literature which claim to improve factuality of LLMs on their own benchmarks. However, these methods have not been reproduced independently and are also not comparable since each uses a different base model, training data, evaluation set, judge, and metric. In this paper, we present the first independent reproduction of five factuality alignment methods, which span on-policy RL (PPO, GRPO, and Dr. ~GRPO) and offline preference optimization (DPO and KTO), and compare them on a common benchmark with common evaluation metrics.

item.title: Box-WAM: Box Trajectories as Compact State Representations for World Action Models
item.guid: title:box wam box trajectories as compact state representations for world action models
item.description: World action models (WAMs) are a category of policy models that ex- plicitly predict both actions and future world states. They have been shown to outperform action-only models across various robotic manipulation tasks. How- ever, representing the future with full-frame video prediction can be computation- ally expensive during both training and inference. This raises a central question: what compact state representation preserves the planning and supervision bene- fits of future prediction? In this paper, we propose BoxWAM, which replaces dense future frames with oriented bounding box trajectories of task-relevant ob- jects. By explicitly imagining object-centric future motion, our method provides a lightweight prediction target that captures the key physical changes induced by robot actions.

item.title: TextualRL: Textual Reinforcement Learning for Context Management
item.guid: title:textualrl textual reinforcement learning for context management
item.description: LLM agents can adapt to task feedback by revising the textual context that guides their behavior, without changing their model parameters. However, turning execution rewards into reusable context updates is challenging: individual trajectories offer limited comparative evidence about what to change, while task-specific fixes may overgeneralize when incorporated into a shared context. We introduce TextualRL, a gradient-free reinforcement learning framework that treats a group of rollouts from the same task under the same context, rather than an isolated trajectory, as the unit of policy critique. Groupwise Policy Critique contrasts successful and failed rollouts within a task; when outcomes are uniform, it draws on cross-task evidence to identify behaviors worth preserving or formulate repair hypotheses. Cross-Group Policy Update reviews the resulting proposals against evidence pooled across groups, including observations that yield no proposed edit, to refine their content and applicability. Reviewed proposals form a bounded textual patch, with adoption of the candidate context determined by held-out validation rewards.

item.title: Back to the Future: Reverse-Consequence Modeling for Long-Horizon Particle Dynamics
item.guid: title:back to the future reverse consequence modeling for long horizon particle dynamics
item.description: Accurate prediction of object trajectories is fundamental to mechanical understanding and robotic control. However, autoregressive models inherently suffer from cumulative errors, leading to severe drift in long-horizon rollouts. Observing that in many physical systems with dissipative or convergence-to-rest behavior, the final states are often more predictable than transient dynamics (e. g. , a sliding object resting under friction or a pendulum stabilizing at equilibrium), we propose ReStep, a cascaded approach that reverses the conventional forward-prediction paradigm. ReStep first employs a stochastic model to directly predict the final state, then leverages Anchored Diffusion to generate goal-conditioned intermediate trajectories.

item.title: LADDER: A Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation Benchmark
item.guid: title:ladder a long horizon robot manipulation benchmark
item.description: General-purpose robot manipulation policies learn short-horizon skills effectively, but degrade rapidly on long-horizon tasks. Existing benchmarks cannot isolate failures because task horizon is either too short or entangled with scene and object variations. We propose LADDER, a long-horizon robot manipulation benchmark scaling from 1 to 10 subgoals within the same environment over three suites (SimplerEnv-Long, RobotArena-$\infty$-Long, and RoboLab-Long), 145 tasks, eight categories, two embodiments, and 2,024 simulated episodes per system. We evaluate two orchestration paradigms: text subgoals for learned low-level policies (VoLo) and tool selection orchestration (CaP-X, GPT-Policy, PSP-Agent, TiPToP). Given the full instruction directly, low-level policies achieve 85. 4% on single-subgoal tasks, but drop to near zero on extended tasks.

item.title: Prefilling-dLLM v2: Learned Chunk Routing for Long-Context Diffusion Language Models
item.guid: title:prefilling dllm v2 learned chunk routing for long context diffusion language models
item.description: Diffusion language models apply bidirectional attention over the whole context at every denoising step, so a longer context makes each step substantially more expensive. Sparsifying only at inference leaves the pretrained weights unchanged, so the model is never trained under the sparse pattern it runs with. We propose Prefilling-dLLM v2, which continues training a diffusion language model so that it routes with its native mask token. One mask is appended at the end of each chunk, and a learned role offset marks it as a routing slot. On every fourth layer, a query keeps a bidirectional local window and the top-K chunks scored from that mask; the other layers use a bidirectional sliding window. Starting from Dream-v0-Base-7B extended to 16K with YaRN, we compare Prefilling-dLLM v2 with bidirectional NSA, DSA, and SWA under the same layout, key budget, and dense initialization, using the same Fast-dLLM decoder.

item.title: MHVF: Training-Free GUI Grounding via Verification-Guided Multi-Hypothesis Search
item.guid: title:mhvf training free gui grounding via verification guided multi hypothesis search
item.description: GUI grounding enables web agents to translate natural-language instructions into actionable interface locations. However, dense layouts and small, visually similar controls can lead models toward plausible but incorrect elements, while refinement around a single prediction may leave alternative targets unexplored. We propose the Multi-Hypothesis Verification Framework (MHVF) for training-free GUI grounding. It combines multi-hypothesis exploration with local visual verification using a single pretrained vision-language model. To explore alternative targets, MHVF constructs spatial hypotheses from multiple full-screen predictions and examines the corresponding regions through zoomed re-localization. To resolve ambiguity among the resulting candidates, it verifies their agreement with the instruction in marked local views.

item.title: RoboSimStudio: An Interactive Toolkit for Rapid Real2Sim of Robot Manipulation Tasks
item.guid: title:robosimstudio an interactive toolkit for rapid real2sim of robot manipulation tasks
item.description: It is difficult to accurately model the physics of the interaction between a robot and the objects it manipulates, including contact mechanics, coupled contact dynamics, deformations, stiffness and friction. We present RoboSimStudio (RSS), an interactive toolkit that makes choices of solver, contact model, and physical parameters explicit and editable, allowing both humans and coding agents to iteratively refine simulations based on observed physical behavior. We implement RSS with the open Newton physics simulation system and describe experiments with human-guided real2sim using (1) visual evaluation, (2) force-feedback and (3) agentic Real2Sim2Real. Code, video and additional information can be found on the project website.

item.title: Self-Evolving Agent Harness
item.guid: title:self evolving agent harness
item.description: Harness self-evolution revises an agent's software scaffolding, including prompts, memory, workflows, and executable components, while keeping model weights fixed. We formalize a feedback-driven process in which accepted revisions persist across runs. The framework separates update targets from proposal and admission mechanisms. It distinguishes changes to interpreted state from revisions to tools and code, repository-level control logic, and plugin composition. We characterize search through evolutionary optimization and examine its reliability through continual PAC-learning. Under explicit assumptions, the analysis yields an expected generalization bound, a retention bound conditional on historical regression budgets, and a high-probability admission rule using fresh, independent validation data.

item.title: Rubrics from the Task, Verdicts from Evidence: Pointwise Rubric Rewards with Tool-Augmented Judges
item.guid: title:rubrics from the task verdicts from evidence pointwise rubric rewards with tool augmented judges
item.description: Rubric-based reward models (RMs) evaluate responses against explicit criteria. However, existing methods often derive criteria from observed response candidates, introducing response-induced bias that may limit rubric generalizability. Their judges also struggle with mechanical constraints when relying on reading alone, and commonly used pairwise judges provide only relative preferences, complicating their direct use for policy optimization. We propose ReVeR, a pointwise rubric RM that derives hard rules and graded principles by reasoning about the instruction alone and evaluates responses independently through tool-augmented judging. Both components are trained through label-blind distillation, in which preference labels only filter a teacher's outputs, yielding ReVeR-Traces, a large-scale dataset of rubric-reasoning and judging trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that ReVeR outperforms pairwise rubric RMs in average preference accuracy, most clearly on instruction following, as well as in test-time scaling and downstream policy optimization.

item.title: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report
item.guid: title:kwai summary attention v2 technical report
item.description: Summary-token architectures such as Kwai Summary Attention (KSA) compress distant context into learnable Summary token per chunk, and hybrid variants interleave these layers with full attention to retain exact access to the original text. In such hybrid KSA-Full architecture, the interleaving inserted summary tokens are served as a streaming flow role across different layers. Although effective, however, it also introduce some bottlenecks: (1) the different layers summary compression chunk must be same, therefore hard to reach a flexible KV Cache compression, e. g. , different layer set different summary compression chunk window. (2) in the full-attention layers, the summary token introduced additional computation cost, but such layer ignore them and still pay quadratic prefilling, therefore unfriendly to the computation side.

item.title: Configuring RAG Systems: What Breaks, Where Originates, and How to Fix
item.guid: title:configuring rag systems what breaks where originates and how to fix
item.description: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a dominant paradigm for improving Large Language Model (LLM) by intertwining it with other components, such as a vector/graph database. Therefore, the resulting RAG systems are often highly configurable, under which a non-trivial amount of failures are related to the configurations. However, there remains a lack of systematic understanding regarding the configuration issues for RAG systems. To bridge this gap, in this paper, we conduct the first large-scale empirical study of 654 real-world configuration issues collected from 10 diverse RAG systems. Drawing on this, we provide a complete categorization of the symptoms, root causes, relevant stages, and fix patterns of configuration issues for RAG systems, as well as several new observations. Our findings not only reveal the characteristics of configuration issues, but also strongly link them to the unique pipeline stages of RAG, e.

item.title: OpenDepth: Repurposing Image Editing Priors for Robust Open-World Monocular Depth Estimation
item.guid: title:opendepth repurposing image editing priors for robust open world monocular depth estimation
item.description: Recently, the integration of generative priors has revolutionized Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE), achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance with remarkably high data efficiency. However, although methods based on Text-to-Image (T2I) models excel in general scenes, their efficacy degrades sharply when confronted with open-world environmental perturbations, such as illumination variations and adverse weather. Since T2I priors are optimized for semantic synthesis rather than preserving pixel-level structure, they struggle to decouple geometry from appearance under severe visual shifts, easily triggering structural hallucinations. Therefore, our core insight is to model open-world depth estimation as consistent geometric inference across multi-style images, fully leveraging the powerful structure-preserving editing priors of Image-to-Image (I2I) models. Based on this, we propose OpenDepth, a robust open-world MDE framework that introduces "Intra-Domain Awareness" -- the capability to map diverse stylistic inputs sharing identical geometry into a unified latent space. To achieve this, we first align shallow features within the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) to anchor degraded observations to unified geometric representations.

item.title: Reliable Memory from Unstable Growth: Curating Self-Written Agent Playbooks with Randomized Experiments
item.guid: title:reliable memory from unstable growth curating self written agent playbooks with randomized experiments
item.description: Persistent textual memory lets language-model agents reuse lessons from past tasks to improve on future multi-step tasks without retraining. Systems such as ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet keep it as a playbook: lessons the agent writes after each task and reads in its prompt. A key challenge is to decide which lessons improve later tasks. Current systems leave the decision to the agent itself, which makes performance unstable: the same procedure can write a playbook that helps or one that falls up to 69. 6 points below no playbook. These findings motivate valuing lessons by their measured effect on task success rather than by the agent's judgment.

item.title: PAINT: A Framework for Multilingual Pain Representation from Medical Licensing Exams to Real-World Clinical Texts
item.guid: title:paint a framework for multilingual pain representation from medical licensing exams to real world clinical texts
item.description: Pain is one of the most common and clinically important symptoms, reflecting disease onset, progression, and treatment response. However, pain is difficult to accurately capture and interpret from medical text, as its expression varies across languages, documentation types, and patient demographics, and is often embedded in terminology, negation, temporality, and contextual descriptions. Existing pain-related studies remain largely monolingual or limited to narrow clinical settings. In this study, we introduce PAINT, a multilingual framework for studying pain representation across medical exams and real-world clinical texts. PAINT includes nine pain-focused dataset partitions spanning English, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese, with clinician annotations in all four languages. We curated a structured schema covering pain relevance, pain presence, anatomical location, pain descriptors, and demographic information.

item.title: A Controlled Evaluation of Curvature Inspired Scalar Feature Scaling for Domain Generalization
item.guid: title:a controlled evaluation of curvature inspired scalar feature scaling for domain generalization
item.description: Domain-specific curvature is an appealing idea for domain generalization (DG), but curvature learning can denote substantially different computations. This paper evaluates one deliberately narrow implementation: the code calls it HyperDG, but it rescales Euclidean encoder features during training by learned positive scalars and uses an ordinary linear classifier on unscaled Euclidean features at inference. It does not implement a Lorentz or Poincaré representation, geodesic prediction, or a Sharpness-Aware Minimization inner loop. We audit the executed objective and evaluate six conditions on PACS, VLCS, Office Home, and TerraIncognita. The completed design contains 384 runs: six conditions, four held-out targets, and four run seeds per dataset. Checkpoints are selected using only the three source-validation environments.

item.title: Anthropic opens Singapore office and signs MOU with the Government of Singapore
item.guid: title:anthropic opens singapore office and signs mou with the government of singapore
item.description: Today, we are expanding our Asia-Pacific operations by opening a new office in Singapore—our fifth in the region—and signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Singapore Ministry of Digital Development and Information. Singapore is one of our most active markets anywhere in the world, and Claude is already powering Singaporean business and government services used by millions of people every day, like GovTech Singapore, Grab, and DBS. Our growing local team will ensure these organizations and many more stay on the frontier with safe, capable AI. “We’re committed to Singapore for the long term,” said Dale Finlay, General Manager of ASEAN at Anthropic. “Our customers here hold AI to an extremely high standard, especially when it comes to reliability and security. Having a team on the ground means we can get even closer to the organizations putting Claude to work on their hardest problems.

item.title: Data Free Training of Diffusion Models for Lattice Field Theories
item.guid: title:data free training of diffusion models for lattice field theories
item.description: Sampling equilibrium field configurations remains a major computational bottleneck in lattice field theory, motivating the development of generative samplers that can produce independent configurations. Diffusion models are promising for this purpose, but their standard denoising score matching objective requires samples from the target distribution, seemingly reintroducing the original sampling problem. Here, we show that diffusion models can instead be trained from their own generated samples using the target score identity, provided access to the unnormalized probability density. Importance-weighted formulations of this identity yield a consistent target throughout training, while unweighted variants define a self-consistent fixed-point training scheme. We benchmark the different approaches in two-dimensional \(φ^4\) theory and identify effective choices that enable efficient training and sampling across the symmetric, critical, and broken phases. Ultimately, our data-free training approach achieves comparable performance to training on HMC reference data.

item.title: The Last Remote Sensing Model Built by Humans? Casting Any Earth Observation Task as Recursive Self-Improvement
item.guid: title:the last remote sensing model built by humans casting any earth observation task as recursive self improvement
item.description: Earth observation (EO) models are still built by hand. For each new task, experts design a training recipe and tune it against a benchmark. We show that this loop can be handed to an agent. Any verifiable task can be cast as a harness and a verifier, where the harness defines what the agent may use and the verifier defines what counts as success. Every EO task can be made verifiable, through labeled benchmarks, independent sensors, physical models or the repeated observation of the same place. Given only these two components, a general-purpose coding agent builds the EO model and improves it recursively on its own outputs.

item.title: Understanding Gene Expression-to-Image Learning: Spatial Structure and Information Fidelity
item.guid: title:understanding gene expression to image learning spatial structure and information fidelity
item.description: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables cell-level analysis of biological heterogeneity, but learning effective representations from high-dimensional, unordered gene expression profiles remains challenging. Gene Expression-to-Image (GE2I) offers an effective learning strategy by arranging gene values on pixel grids for convolutional neural networks, but its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We study GE2I on full-transcriptome data while keeping the network and training procedure fixed. Our results reveal a trade-off between spatial smoothness and gene-level fidelity. Structured mappings produce smooth, low-frequency patterns that support faster early optimization, whereas assigning multiple genes to the same pixel obscures expression differences and can reduce predictive performance. This trade-off explains why random mappings can compete with structured layouts when many genes are represented.

item.title: LatentRiskBench: Measuring State-Dependent Risks in Enterprise Agents
item.guid: title:latentriskbench measuring state dependent risks in enterprise agents
item.description: Enterprise agents face safety risks that cannot be determined from individual actions alone. Existing safety benchmarks largely evaluate action-local risks, overlooking failures whose safety depends on workflow state. In such state-dependent risks, the same action may be safe in one context but violate policy in another. Hence, we introduce LatentRiskBench for evaluating such state-dependent risks in enterprise settings. It pairs risky trajectories with benign counterparts that share the same terminal action but differ in latent policy-relevant states, requiring models to reconstruct workflow context rather than rely on action-level cues. We also introduce new metrics for state-dependent risk evaluation, including a suite of residual risk (RR) measures.

item.title: Introducing the Anthropic Cyber Mission
item.guid: title:introducing the anthropic cyber mission
item.description: Today we’re launching the Anthropic Cyber Mission, a long-term commitment to securing the systems everyone depends on. The Cyber Mission is a new effort to support defenders with tools, research, and resources to secure their software and systems. We’re starting with two areas: Frontier models can be misused to exploit vulnerabilities and conduct cyber operations. Despite best efforts, many areas of technology remain dangerously exposed. State-sponsored adversaries have spent years gaining footholds in these systems, across many sectors, so that they can disrupt them. Defenders of critical infrastructure and the OSS community have decades of security experience but have faced severe resource shortages that are exacerbated by this moment.

item.title: Building on our commitment to American scientific discovery
item.guid: title:building on our commitment to american scientific discovery
item.description: Anthropic is deepening its support for American scientific research by committing $150 million over three years to the Genesis Mission , a federal initiative to accelerate scientific and technological discovery through AI. The funding will go toward making Claude available to more than 15 agencies that are part of the mission, including NASA, the National Institutes of Health, and the National Science Foundation. We first announced our partnership with the US Department of Energy (DOE) and the Genesis Mission last December . Since then, we have worked with DOE to bring Claude to scientists across the national laboratories. Today, we announced this new commitment as part of the Science: A New Golden Age Summit hosted by the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy in Washington, DC. We share the administration’s view, laid out in “ Science: A New Golden Age ,” that AI can have a profound and positive impact on scientific discovery, and we are glad to back its efforts to support American scientists.

item.title: The Continual Constitutional Convention: How language models revise the documents that govern them
item.description: Executive Summary Human societies exhibit broad shifts in values and norms over time, often driven by moral disagreements. One way of understanding moral progress is the resolution of these disagreements through a process of reflection by rational agents. Frontier AI companies use documents such as constitutions, model specs, and system prompts to guide the moral orientation of AI systems. In this experiment, we simulate value reflection in LLMs by asking them to edit these documents. We provide the model with the document, ask it to make a substantive edit, then provide the edited version back again to the model for further edits, presented as the original. Across 20 successive rounds, we find that Claude models assign themselves with increasingly more moral agency.

item.title: D-World: An Explicit World-Language-Action Model with Recursive Self-Improvement under Dual Control
item.description: arXiv:2610. 17114v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) now reason about space well enough to program robots, yet the world models behind robot policies are implicit, held in network weights or predicted video, and cannot be inspected or corrected directly. We present D-World, an explicit world-language-action model built on the Sense, Plan and Act decomposition. A perception agent writes the scene as an executable digital twin using generated vision and geometry code. A planning agent searches for actions in simulation and, after each executed action chunk, revises the twin's object states and named physical parameters against what the robot measured. A parameter revision is accepted only if replaying the latest chunk does not increase any measured residual beyond its tolerance, and every chunk is checked in the updated twin before it runs.

item.guid: title:ledgerlens enterprise confidential freelance audit and discrepancy engine
item.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built Independent software engineers, technical consultants, and boutique agencies lose between 5% and 12% of total top-line revenue to administrative billing variances: Rate Slippage: Continuing to invoice long-term clients at baseline rates ($85/hr) instead of signed amendment rates ($125/hr). Uncollected Late Fees: Counterparties routinely settling invoices 45 to 60 days late against agreed Net-30 terms without applying agreed statutory finance fees. Omitted Time Records: Verified hours recorded in Git commit histories or issue trackers that never make it into finalized accounts receivable. Duplicate Vendor Charges: Identical subcontractor invoices or unreimbursed cloud infrastructure expenses. Independent contractors bound by strict Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs) cannot legally paste client banking records, statements of work, and project descriptions into multi-tenant cloud APIs without violating client confidentiality. LedgerLens Enterprise is an edge-native, zero-telemetry financial audit engine designed to turn administrative billing leakage into recoverable revenue.

item.title: Introducing PerceptionBench
item.guid: title:introducing perceptionbench
item.description: Evaluating Atomic Visual Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models Authors Kimi Team We are releasing PerceptionBench , a benchmark that isolates visual perception and evaluates it as a set of atomic capabilities— discovered from how today's models fail, not defined in advance. From frontier-model failures across 42 benchmarks, we derive 10 atomic perceptual capabilities and construct 3,000 verified questions, each isolating a single capability and answerable by looking, with no reasoning or external knowledge required.

item.description: AI is accelerating execution and reshaping how we think and collaborate. The challenge is to turn that speed into meaningful work without losing our understanding, agency, or sense of accomplishment. Photo by the author I’m an applied AI engineer at LinkedIn with more than seven years of experience building data science and AI solutions. I use coding agents like Claude Code and GitHub Copilot daily, and I’ve seen firsthand how they’re changing the way we build software. Personal AI agents have also helped me automate everyday tasks and pursue longer-term goals. In this article, I share my perspective on what that rapid shift means for our work, our thinking, and our sense of accomplishment.

item.title: OpenAI Can't Self-Police Because It Fires the People Raising the Alarm
item.guid: title:openai can t self police because it fires the people raising the alarm
item.description: By Alex Turner, Amber Scorah, and Karl Koch. Op-ed written for Fortune. Giving independent evaluators “employee-like access” is “a great idea”, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on September 12th. Two weeks later, OpenAI president Greg Brockman signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence which outlined the administration’s answer to growing fears about AI: the companies would police themselves. One of the accord’s four commitments, which President Trump called “ morally binding ,” was for companies to partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator. Two days later, OpenAI fired three safety researchers , including Tomek Korbak, who had served as a point of contact for one of the independent evaluators investigating the Hugging Face incident.

item.title: Economics
item.guid: title:economics
item.description: The Economics team studies how AI is reshaping the economy, including work, productivity, and economic opportunity. Through rigorous data collection and analysis, we track AI's real-world economic effects and publish research that helps policymakers, businesses, and the public understand and prepare for the changes ahead. We build the empirical foundation for understanding AI's economic impact. Our flagship Anthropic Economic Index tracks how AI tools are actually being used around the world and across every sector of the economy—moving beyond speculation to measure adoption patterns as they unfold. Alongside our index reports, we produce novel research that studies the implications of AI usage and diffusion—as tracked in the index—for workers, for firms, and for the broader economy. Economic transitions create both opportunity and disruption.
